outputs.L1:
In the present paper, we propose a seemingly new method for finding closed-form solutions to certain types of nonlinear PDEs. The method is based on the decomposition of nonlinear operators into a sequence of lower-order operators. It is shown that the decomposition process can be carried out by iterative procedures, each step of which is reduced to solving certain auxiliary systems of PDEs for a single dependent variable. Moreover, in this way we obtain an explicit expression for the first-order PDEs governing the first integrals of the decomposable initial PDE. Remarkably, these first-order PDEs are linear if the initial PDE is linear in its highest-order derivatives.

The developed method is implemented as a Maple procedure, which can effectively solve many PDEs of different orders and with different numbers of independent variables. Examples of PDEs together with their computed general solutions demonstrate the potential of the method for the automatic solution of nonlinear PDEs.
outputs.L2:
In this paper, we present what appears to be a new approach for obtaining closed-form solutions to certain classes of nonlinear partial differential equations. The approach relies on representing nonlinear differential operators as a sequence of lower-order operators. We show that this factorization can be carried out through iterative procedures, where each stage is reduced to solving auxiliary systems of PDEs involving a single dependent variable. In addition, this process yields an explicit form of the first-order PDEs associated with a first integral of the original decomposable PDE. Notably, when the original equation is linear with respect to its highest-order derivatives, the resulting first-order PDE is also linear.

The proposed method has been implemented as a Maple procedure and is capable of solving many PDEs of various orders and with different numbers of independent variables. Examples in which general solutions are computed illustrate the method’s promise for the automated solution of nonlinear partial differential equations.
outputs.L3:
The paper proposes a seemingly new method for finding closed-form solutions to certain classes of nonlinear partial differential equations. Rather than attempting to solve the original equation directly, the approach focuses on identifying structural properties of the differential operator that defines the PDE. In particular, the method is based on decomposing nonlinear operators into sequences of lower-order operators. This decomposition can simplify the original problem by breaking it into smaller and more manageable components.

A central idea of the paper is that the decomposition process can be carried out iteratively. At each stage, the problem is reduced to solving auxiliary systems of partial differential equations involving a single dependent variable. This iterative reduction provides a systematic way to uncover intermediate relations, or first integrals, that help lower the effective order or complexity of the original PDE. As a result, the method offers a constructive path toward obtaining exact solutions.

The authors also derive explicit first-order partial differential equations for the first integrals associated with decomposable initial PDEs. These equations play an important role in the method because they characterize the quantities that remain invariant under the action of the decomposed operators. An important feature is that when the original PDE is linear with respect to its highest-order derivatives, the resulting first-order PDEs for the first integrals are themselves linear. This makes the auxiliary problems significantly easier to solve and broadens the practical applicability of the approach.

To demonstrate the usefulness of the method, the authors implement it as a procedure in Maple. Through a range of examples, they show that the algorithm can find solutions for PDEs of different orders and involving different numbers of independent variables. These examples illustrate both the flexibility and the computational feasibility of the decomposition technique. Overall, the paper presents a structured and algorithmic framework for deriving closed-form solutions to certain nonlinear PDEs by reducing them to sequences of lower-order problems.

The paper presents a new method for obtaining closed-form solutions of a class of nonlinear partial differential equations. The central idea is to decompose a nonlinear differential operator into a sequence of simpler, lower-order operators. This decomposition is constructed through an iterative procedure involving auxiliary systems of partial differential equations. By reducing the original problem step by step, the method transforms the task of solving a higher-order nonlinear PDE into the solution of a sequence of lower-order equations.

A key contribution of the paper is the derivation of explicit first-order partial differential equations for the first integrals associated with the given PDE. These first integrals play a crucial role in lowering the order of the original equation and in building the operator decomposition. In the important special case where the original PDE is linear with respect to its highest-order derivatives, the corresponding equations for the first integrals are themselves linear. This makes the method especially effective, since linear first-order PDEs are often significantly easier to analyze and solve than the original nonlinear equation.

The authors also describe a computer implementation of the method in Maple. This implementation automates much of the decomposition process and is able to solve many examples of partial differential equations without manual intervention. The computational results demonstrate that the method can successfully handle a broad range of PDEs, including nonlinear cases that are difficult for standard symbolic solvers. Overall, the paper shows that decomposing nonlinear operators into lower-order components provides a promising and practical approach to the closed-form solution of nonlinear partial differential equations.
outputs.L5:
PDEs, or partial differential equations, are fundamental tools in mathematics, physics, engineering, and many applied sciences. The study of PDEs helps describe complex phenomena such as heat flow, wave motion, fluid dynamics, and electromagnetic fields. These equations involve functions of several variables and their partial derivatives, making them essential for modeling systems that change across both space and time.

The importance of PDEs lies in their ability to translate real-world processes into precise mathematical language. For example, the heat equation models how temperature spreads through a material, while the wave equation describes vibrations, sound, and light propagation. By solving PDEs, scientists and engineers can predict behavior, optimize designs, and better understand natural laws.

Moreover, PDEs are not only useful in classical science but also in modern fields such as image processing, financial mathematics, machine learning, and climate modeling. Their wide range of applications makes them one of the most powerful and versatile areas of mathematical study.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematical paper introducing a new Maple-implemented method for solving nonlinear PDEs by decomposing differential operators into lower-order operators.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a Maple-implemented symbolic method for constructing exact solutions of nonlinear partial differential equations by decomposing their differential operators into compositions of lower-order operators. The approach rewrites a given nonlinear PDE, or a system of PDEs, in an operator-decomposition form and systematically derives auxiliary lower-order equations whose solutions generate solutions of the original problem. The method combines symbolic factorization, differential substitution, compatibility checking, and simplification procedures, allowing nonlinear terms and variable coefficients to be treated within a unified computational framework.

The implementation automates the search for admissible decompositions, determines the associated constraints on parameters or coefficient functions, and returns reduced equations of lower differential order. These reduced equations are often more tractable and may yield explicit exact solutions, solution families, or integrability conditions. The algorithm is designed to work directly with Maple’s symbolic differentiation and algebraic manipulation capabilities, making it suitable for interactive exploration as well as automated computation.

Several examples are presented to illustrate the method, including nonlinear evolution equations and multidimensional PDEs. The computations demonstrate that operator decomposition can recover known exact solutions and produce new solution forms under suitable parameter restrictions. The Maple procedures provide a practical tool for researchers studying nonlinear PDEs, complementing existing methods such as symmetry reductions, Darboux transformations, and direct ansatz-based techniques.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract for a paper on automatic symbolic solution of PDEs, where nonlinear PDE operators are iteratively decomposed and auxiliary PDE systems are solved.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a symbolic framework for the automatic solution of nonlinear partial differential equations based on iterative operator decomposition and the solution of auxiliary PDE systems. The proposed method represents a given nonlinear PDE operator as a structured composition of simpler differential and algebraic components, enabling systematic reduction of the original problem into a sequence of auxiliary equations. At each iteration, candidate decompositions are generated symbolically, compatibility conditions are derived, and intermediate PDE systems are solved or simplified using differential elimination, ansatz construction, and integrability analysis. The resulting solutions are then propagated through the decomposition chain to reconstruct exact solutions of the original nonlinear problem.

The framework is designed to operate without requiring a problem-specific ansatz, while still allowing domain knowledge to guide the search when available. It supports nonlinearities involving products, powers, and composite differential expressions, and can identify transformations that reduce nonlinear PDEs to linear or lower-order auxiliary systems. We discuss the algorithmic structure of the method, criteria for selecting useful decompositions, and strategies for controlling expression growth. Several examples demonstrate that the approach recovers known exact solutions and produces new symbolic solution families for representative nonlinear evolution and stationary PDEs. The results suggest that iterative symbolic decomposition provides a flexible and extensible route toward automated exact solution generation for nonlinear PDEs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an old-fashioned mathematical abstract about a seemingly new technique for solving nonlinear PDEs in closed form, emphasizing decomposition into lower-order operators and examples of general solutions.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**—In this note we describe a rather elementary method, apparently not much exploited, for obtaining closed-form solutions of certain non-linear partial differential equations. The method consists in replacing the given equation, whenever possible, by a succession of equations of lower order, the corresponding differential operators being chosen so as to factor the original expression modulo an integrable remainder. Thus, instead of attacking directly an equation of the form  
\[
F(x,u,Du,D^2u,\ldots,D^nu)=0,
\]
one seeks a decomposition
\[
\mathcal F=\mathcal L_1\mathcal L_2\cdots \mathcal L_k+\mathcal R,
\]
where the operators \(\mathcal L_i\) are of lower order, often first order, and where \(\mathcal R\) either vanishes on the successive kernels or is absorbed by a suitable quadrature.

The procedure is especially transparent in the case where the nonlinear terms admit a hidden divergence form or may be rendered separable after the introduction of an auxiliary dependent variable. In this way several familiar equations appear as members of a single class. For example, equations reducible to
\[
(\partial_x-a(u)\partial_y)(\partial_x-b(u)\partial_y)u=0
\]
lead at once to a pair of characteristic systems, and their general integral is expressible in terms of two arbitrary functions. Similarly, certain nonlinear wave equations may be written symbolically as
\[
(\partial_t-c(u)\partial_x)(\partial_t+c(u)\partial_x)u=G(u,Du),
\]
where the right-hand term is chosen so that it is cancelled along the intermediate characteristic foliation.

As illustrations, we indicate the recovery of general solutions of model equations such as  
\[
u_{xy}=A(u)u_xu_y,
\]
for which the substitution
\[
v=\int^u e^{-\int^s A(r)\,dr}\,ds
\]
reduces the equation to \(v_{xy}=0\), giving
\[
\int^u e^{-\int^s A(r)\,dr}\,ds=\phi(x)+\psi(y),
\]
with \(\phi,\psi\) arbitrary. We also mention equations of generalized Riccati type in which a nonlinear second-order operator is decomposed into two first-order Riccati operators, yielding solutions through linear equations and quadratures.

The chief point of the paper is not the discovery of isolated transformations, but the systematic use of operator decomposition as a calculus for detecting them. The resulting formulae furnish, in favourable cases, complete integrals depending upon arbitrary functions, and hence closed-form general solutions. The method is formal in character, yet it gives a simple unifying explanation for a number of classical reductions and suggests new ones for nonlinear equations whose solvability is otherwise obscure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
